content: RaiSE draws a sharp distinction between two categories of work: delivery work and management work.
Delivery work is one of the two categories of work distinguished in RaiSE.
Management work is one of the two categories of work distinguished in RaiSE.
Delivery work has different workflows.
Management work has different workflows.
Delivery work has different success criteria.
Management work has different success criteria.
Delivery work has different accountability models.
Management work has different accountability models.

Delivery work produces observable value for end users. It is the reason the team exists. Delivery work follows TDD, has acceptance criteria, and produces something a user can interact with, measure, or depend on.
Stories implementing a new feature
Bugfixes that correct user-facing defects
Epics that deliver a new capability
Performance improvements with measurable user impact
Follows the canonical lifecycle (start → design → plan → implement → review → close)
Requires TDD (tests first, always)
Has formal acceptance criteria (Gherkin scenarios)
Produces a retrospective with extracted patterns
Tracked in the delivery project in Jira (Story/Bug issue types)

Management work is necessary for delivery to happen, but it does not directly produce user-facing value. It is overhead — necessary overhead, but overhead nonetheless. RaiSE tracks management work to make its cost visible, not to treat it as value.
Compliance documentation (GDPR, SOC 2, audit reports)
Infrastructure maintenance (not tied to a feature)
Team coordination meetings with action items
Reporting and dashboards
Hiring and onboarding coordination
Tool setup and administration
Does not follow TDD (no test-driven requirement)
Does not require acceptance criteria (operational outcomes, not user outcomes)
Uses Task issue type in Jira
May or may not have a retrospective (depends on the task)
Tracked in a management project or as management tasks within delivery projects
a bounded software initiative
a bounded administrative initiative
A compliance audit epic is a management epic.
A new authentication system epic is a delivery epic.
The distinction is not always obvious — the test is: "Does this directly produce something a user interacts with?"
Mixing delivery and management work in the same backlog without distinction inflates apparent velocity (points moved) while masking real delivery throughput.
Delivery work has observable outcomes (working software). Management work has operational outcomes (document written, meeting held). The accountability models differ.

The right process for each type of work is different. Applying TDD and acceptance criteria to compliance documentation creates unnecessary friction. Omitting TDD from a feature story creates quality debt.
Autonomous agents should focus on delivery work. Management work often requires human judgment and authority that agents should not assume. RaiSE's pipeline engine is optimized for delivery work.
RaiSE's pipeline engine is optimized for delivery work.
Test-Driven Development.
Some work is hybrid — it has both delivery and management dimensions.
a monitoring dashboard is delivery work (users interact with it) but its primary purpose is management (tracking team health).
In these cases, classify by the primary value driver.
When in doubt: ask "Who is the user?"
If the user is an end customer, it is delivery.
If the user is the team itself, it is management.
value work vs overhead
delivery vs admin
productive vs operational
feature work vs process work
direct value vs supporting value
Dependencies in RaiSE come in two forms: work dependencies (one story depends on another) and technical dependencies (one component depends on another).
Managing both work and technical dependencies well is critical for delivery predictability.
one story depends on another
one component depends on another
Work that must be completed before the current work can start or complete. In RaiSE, upstream dependencies are documented in the story scope and tracked via Jira issue links ("is blocked by").
The current story cannot start without the upstream being done. Example: a story implementing a feature that requires a database schema migration from another story.
The current story can start but cannot complete without the upstream. Example: a UI story that can be built against a mock but needs the real API to be validated.
Phase where hard upstream dependencies must be resolved before the story enters.
Phase where soft upstream dependencies must be resolved before the story enters.

Work that depends on the current work. The current story "unblocks" the downstream. RaiSE tracks these with "blocks" Jira links. These should be prioritized because blocking them costs more than just the story's own delay.
When a story in one epic depends on a story from another epic. These are the most dangerous because they cross team boundaries and planning horizons.

These should be minimized by: decomposing epics around vertical slices (each slice is independently shippable), using interface-first design (define the contract before implementing either side), and explicit coordination via the mission planning level.
Decomposing epics such that each slice is independently shippable.
Define the contract before implementing either side.
Explicit coordination via the mission planning level.
External packages (Python packages via uv, npm packages, etc.) are technical dependencies.
RaiSE's supply chain gate requires evaluating new external dependencies before introducing them: version history, download count, maintenance status, bus factor, yank history.

metadata.verification: evaluation of external dependencies based on version history, download count, maintenance status, bus factor, yank history

content: Well-known packages (pydantic, fastapi, pytest, typer) are pre-approved.
Novel packages require evaluation.
Internal dependencies (one module importing from another) create coupling.

The direction of coupling matters: stable modules (core abstractions, graph models) should not import from volatile modules (new features, experimental code). Coupling in the wrong direction creates fragility.
RaiSE's architecture review checks coupling direction as part of the systemic audit.
External services (databases, APIs, message queues) are runtime dependencies.
Stories that introduce new service dependencies should document: the service's SLA, the fallback behavior when the service is unavailable, and the health check strategy.

metadata.verification: documentation includes service SLA, fallback behavior, and health check strategy

content: Depend on abstractions, not concretions. Define an interface first, implement it second. This allows parallel development (one team implements the interface, another consumes it) and easier testing (mock the interface, not the implementation).

When a story has upstream dependencies that are not yet complete, build the walking skeleton against mocks. The walking skeleton demonstrates the end-to-end flow without requiring all components to be production-ready.

When two stories have a soft dependency, use a feature flag to allow the upstream to merge first (with the flag off) and the downstream to integrate later (with the flag on). This avoids long-lived branches.
List upstream dependencies (what this story depends on) and downstream dependencies (what this story unblocks).
The `dependencies` field lists what the story depends on and whether it is a blocker.
Use "is blocked by" and "blocks" link types to make dependencies visible in the board view.
Cross-story dependencies are documented in the Implementation Plan section with the sequencing rationale.

The standard progression for delivery work in RaiSE. It applies to stories, bugfixes, and epics (with phase-specific variations).
Skipping phases in the canonical lifecycle is not a shortcut, it is a process defect.
The start phase initializes the work unit: creates the branch, writes the scope document, transitions the backlog item to in-progress, and binds the work to the session.
The scope commit is a hard gate — no implementation work happens on an unbranched story.
For stories: `/rai-story-start` creates `story/s{N}.{M}/{slug}` from the development branch, writes `scope.md` and `story.md`, transitions Jira to the design status.
For epics: `/rai-epic-start` initializes `work/epics/e{N}-{name}/`, creates `scope.md`, transitions the epic ticket.

Design is the gemba walk — going to the actual code before deciding what to build. Design without reading the code is guessing. The design document captures: problem, value, approach, affected components, decisions, examples, and acceptance criteria.
Design is never optional. A story that skips design is likely to build the wrong thing or duplicate existing functionality.
The design HITL gate requires human approval before proceeding to plan.
The design document captures: problem, value, approach, affected components, decisions, examples, and acceptance criteria.
Output: `design.md` (structured artifact + Markdown view + Confluence page)

The plan decomposes the story into atomic, individually verifiable tasks. Each task has: description, files affected, TDD cycle (RED → GREEN → REFACTOR), acceptance criteria reference, verification commands with explicit scope, and size estimate.
The plan determines execution order (risk-first), identifies dependencies (sequential vs parallel).
The plan includes the Gate Policy (how to run tests — always via `rai gate check`, never directly via pytest or npm test).
Output: `plan.md`

Implementation follows the plan task by task. Each task completes its full TDD cycle before moving to the next. No task is considered done until gates pass: tests, lint, format, types. Each completed task gets its own commit.
Each task completes its full TDD cycle before moving to the next.
No task is considered done until gates pass: tests, lint, format, types.

The review phase is an adversarial retrospective. It includes: architecture review (proportionality, YAGNI, Beck's four rules), quality review (semantic bugs, type honesty, test quality), and pattern extraction (what was learned that should propagate to future stories).
architecture review (proportionality, YAGNI, Beck's four rules)
quality review (semantic bugs, type honesty, test quality)
pattern extraction (what was learned that should propagate to future stories)
The architecture review asks: "Could we achieve the same outcome with less?"
The quality review asks: "What did the automated gates miss?"
Both are required before close.

Close merges the story branch to the development branch, updates the epic progress tracking, transitions the Jira issue to Done, and emits the lifecycle signal. The retrospective document is committed before merge.
For epics: close includes the epic retrospective, architecture doc update, and merge of the epic accumulation branch.
Scope commit on story branch
HITL design approval
HITL plan approval (adversarial AR + QR in pipeline)

Retrospective document complete
The initial phase of a project.
The phase where design decisions are made.
The phase where the plan is developed.
The phase where the plan is implemented.
The phase where work is reviewed.
The final phase of a project, closing out work.
Gates are not bureaucracy — they are quality checkpoints.
"Move fast" by passing gates, not by skipping them.
start → design → plan → [stories iterate] → close. Stories execute their full 6-phase lifecycle within the epic container.
start → triage → analyse → plan → fix → review → close → PIR. The PIR (post-incident review) is an additional phase that extracts systemic lessons.
Compressed bugfix lifecycle for production incidents. Same phases, accelerated timeline. RCA is required but may be done after the fix is deployed (with a commitment to complete it).
An additional phase for bugfix lifecycles that extracts systemic lessons.
RCA is required for hotfixes but may be done after the fix is deployed (with a commitment to complete it).

Metrics in RaiSE measure the health of the delivery process, not just its output. A team that ships fast but accumulates technical debt, skips retrospectives, or burns out engineers is not healthy. RaiSE tracks metrics that capture the full picture.
Health of the delivery process.
Technical debt accumulated by a team.
Skipping retrospectives.
Engineers burning out.
Story points completed per sprint (typically 2 weeks). Sum of points on stories transitioned to Done during the sprint period.

Time from "work started" (scope commit) to "work done" (branch merged) for a single story. `done_at - started_at` for each story. Tracked per story, aggregated per sprint. Cycle time reveals process bottlenecks.

Time from "story created in backlog" to "story done." Includes queue time. `done_at - created_at`. Longer than cycle time because it includes the waiting period. Lead time tells stakeholders how long it takes from request to delivery.
Percentage of bugs that were not caught during implementation and reached review or production. `bugs_caught_in_review / total_bugs` and `bugs_in_production / total_bugs`.
RaiSE's gate policy (tests + lint + types before review) is designed to minimize escape rate.

Average number of new patterns extracted per story retrospective. A team that learns from every story improves compoundingly. A team that skips retrospectives or writes empty ones stagnates. Low pattern rate is a signal to improve retrospective quality.

metadata.verification: Count of patterns registered (PAT-E-*) per story, averaged over the sprint.

content: Percentage of gate check runs that pass on first attempt. Low gate pass rate indicates: TDD not being followed (writing code before tests), rushed implementation, or gate infrastructure problems. Target: >80% first-try pass rate.

Percentage of stories that complete a design document before implementation. Design compliance is a leading indicator of rework rates. Stories without design have 2-3x higher rework rates based on empirical observation.

metadata.verification: Stories with design.md committed before the first implementation commit.

content: Number of implementation attempts before a story passes review. Target: ≤2 attempts. More than 2 suggests the design or planning phase has issues.
Time between an HITL gate being presented and a human approving or rejecting it. Target: ≤5 minutes per decision. Longer indicates gates are not being monitored or decisions are unclear.

Percentage of stories completed without escalation beyond HITL gates. Use: Measures the reliability of autonomous execution. High escalation rate suggests the agent is encountering novel situations not covered by patterns.
A gate that requires Human-In-The-Loop (HITL) for a decision.
Metrics are sensors, not targets. Track metrics to understand the system, not to optimize the metric.
Goodhart's Law applies: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.
RaiSE emits telemetry signals at lifecycle transitions (start, design-complete, implement-complete, etc.) that feed dashboards.
The signals are observational — they do not gate the process.

RaiSE uses natural language queries to retrieve relevant knowledge from its graph and cartridges.
RaiSE maintains synonym mappings to ensure retrieval is robust to terminology variation, because the same concept can be expressed in many ways across teams and organizations.

Retro, retrospective, review session, post-mortem, after-action review, lessons learned, sprint review, story close review. All of these terms refer to the structured reflection at the end of a work unit that extracts learnings and patterns. In RaiSE, retrospectives produce: pattern candidates, improvement actions, and a committed retrospective.md document.

Decision, ADR, architecture decision record, design decision, trade-off, architectural choice, tech decision. Decisions are captured in governance/adrs/ as numbered ADR documents. They follow the format: context, decision, rationale, consequences. ADRs are binding — a decision recorded in an ADR is not relitigated without a new ADR superseding it.
ADRs are binding — a decision recorded in an ADR is not relitigated without a new ADR superseding it.

Blocked, impediment, blocker, stuck, waiting, dependency, bottleneck, constraint. A blocked item cannot proceed. Blocked status requires a documented reason and resolution path. In Jira, blocked items should have a link to the blocking issue and a comment explaining what needs to happen.

Epic, initiative, feature set, capability, program increment, large story, theme. An epic is a multi-story work container. Not to be confused with a Jira Epic (which is a specific issue type) — in RaiSE, the concept maps to Jira Epics but the semantics are richer.

Story, user story, feature, requirement, deliverable, ticket, issue, card. A story is the unit of delivery. In Jira, stories are Story-type issues. In conversation, "feature" and "requirement" often mean the same thing. "Ticket" is a colloquialism that maps to story in delivery contexts.

Plan, decomposition, task breakdown, sprint plan, implementation plan, execution plan. A plan decomposes a story into atomic tasks. In RaiSE, the plan document contains ordered tasks with TDD guidance and gate policy.

Scope, boundaries, in-scope/out-of-scope, done-when, acceptance criteria, definition of done. Scope defines what is and isn't part of a work unit. The scope document (scope.md) contains three sections: In Scope, Out of Scope, Done When. Done-when is functionally equivalent to "definition of done" in Scrum terminology.

Workflow, process, lifecycle, pipeline, SDLC, delivery process. The canonical lifecycle (start → design → plan → implement → review → close) is the workflow. "Pipeline" refers both to the lifecycle and to the automation pipeline (MCP pipeline engine) that orchestrates skill invocations.

Pattern, practice, convention, best practice, established approach, known solution. Patterns are extractable, reusable solutions to recurring problems. They are stored in the pattern system (PAT-E-*) and propagated via retrospectives. A pattern is not a rule — it is a documented solution that worked in a specific context.

Metric, measurement, KPI, indicator, signal, telemetry. Metrics measure the health of the delivery process. Key metrics in RaiSE: story points per sprint (velocity), cycle time (start to done), defect escape rate (bugs that reach review/prod), retrospective pattern rate (patterns extracted per story).

A glossary is a list of terms specific to a particular domain, subject, or text, along with their definitions.
A terminology map outlines the relationships between different terms and concepts within a specific field.

Domain vocabulary refers to the specialized set of terms and words used within a particular field or industry.
Risk management in RaiSE is practical and embedded in the delivery process — not a separate discipline that produces documents nobody reads.
Risks are captured at the epic and story level.
Risks are assessed by probability and impact.
Risks are mitigated through specific technical decisions.
Likely to occur based on past experience, known technical constraints, or environmental factors.
Could occur; some evidence or precedent exists.
Unlikely but worth noting; would be a surprise if it occurred.
Blocks delivery, requires significant rework, or affects production users.
Causes delays or requires moderate rework but doesn't block.
Minor friction; easily mitigated or absorbed.

Risks are registered in three places: Epic scope, Story design, and Architecture review.
A "Riesgos" section with the top 3 risks for the epic, their probability/impact/mitigation.
The `drift_risks` section captures risks specific to the technical approach — particularly AG4 (context-window planning) and AG2 (clone amplification).
The AR identifies systemic risks (orphaned abstractions, coupling direction, shotgun surgery).
AG4 (context-window planning) is a technical approach risk.
AG2 (clone amplification) is a technical approach risk.
Orphaned abstractions are systemic risks identified in Architecture Review.
Coupling direction is a systemic risk identified in Architecture Review.
Shotgun surgery is a systemic risk identified in Architecture Review.
For high-technical-risk stories, implement the riskiest component first as a minimal proof-of-concept before building the full feature. This surfaces blockers early when rework is cheap.

Large epics with high scope risk should be sliced into smaller stories that can be delivered and validated independently. A story that delivers partial value is better than a large story that delivers no value until it's complete.

Isolate external dependencies (APIs, services, databases) behind interfaces so that mock implementations can be used during development and testing. This prevents external instability from blocking the team.
For non-deterministic components (LLM extraction, ML models), commit extracted artifacts as frozen fixtures. This prevents re-extraction surprises and ensures tests are deterministic.

When a risk materializes during implementation (a gate fails unexpectedly, an assumption proves wrong), escalate to the HITL gate pattern: stop, document the finding, propose options, wait for human decision. Do not push forward blindly.
Stop, document the finding, propose options, wait for human decision.
Risks are tracked where the work is tracked — in the epic scope, story design, and retrospective.
Risks are tracked in the epic scope.

Process improvement actions are derived from materialized risks from retrospectives.
A risk that materializes and was not in the risk register is a signal to improve the risk identification process.
Capture as a pattern: 'In the context of X, we missed risk Y. In future, look for Y when doing X.'

A roadmap in RaiSE is not a Gantt chart or a commitment to dates. It is a sequenced set of intentions — what the team plans to build, in what order, and why — with enough granularity to coordinate across teams but not so much detail that it becomes outdated as soon as it is written.

A mission is a teleological container — it defines a bounded initiative with explicit objectives and success criteria. Missions span multiple epics and potentially multiple quarters. They are the highest planning level in RaiSE.
A mission has: a name, a set of objectives (each with observable completion criteria), a set of linked epics, and a timeline horizon.
Mission: Retrieval híbrido neuro-simbólico — Objectives: (1) federated retrieval across 3 cartridges, (2) hybrid ranking with symbolic + neural scores, (3) quota tier enforcement.
An epic translates a mission objective into a bounded deliverable. Epics are the primary planning unit for quarterly planning.
An epic has: a scope document, a design document, a plan with story sequence, and a retrospective at close.
An epic is sized by the sum of its stories (roughly 8–40+ points). A well-planned epic can be delivered in 1–4 sprints.
Planning artifacts: `work/epics/e{N}-{name}/scope.md`, `design.md`, `scope.md` (updated with progress tracking).

Stories are the unit of planning within a sprint. Sprint planning selects stories from the ready queue (stories with design completed and estimated), orders them by priority and dependency, and assigns them to the sprint.
Story-level planning is done in Jira (sprint board) and in the session (daily focus).
The session journal captures intra-day decisions that don't warrant a Jira comment.
A roadmap is a set of intentions, not a commitment. Reality changes: requirements shift, technical constraints emerge, priorities change. A roadmap that cannot change is a liability, not an asset.

RaiSE separates roadmap change from delivery commitment: a sprint commitment (the stories selected for the current sprint) is a short-term commitment. A quarterly roadmap is a medium-term intention. A mission is a long-term direction.
When the roadmap needs to change: document why (ADR or mission update), adjust the epic/story sequence, communicate the change to stakeholders.

A stakeholder is anyone who has a stake in the outcome of a work item — they either influence what gets built, depend on what gets built, or are accountable for its quality.
RaiSE recognizes several categories of stakeholders, each with different roles in the delivery process.

The developer is the primary user of RaiSE. They work directly with the CLI, invoke skills, run gates, and produce the delivery artifacts. Developers are the agents of the canonical lifecycle — they start stories, design them, implement them, and close them.

In the RaiSE model, developers operate at different mastery levels (ShuHaRi): Shu (learning, needs guidance), Ha (competent, adapts patterns), Ri (expert, creates patterns). The coaching model adjusts verbosity and explanation depth based on mastery level.

Every work item in RaiSE has a status that communicates its current state in the lifecycle. Status is not cosmetic — it drives automation, reporting, and process gates. Using a status incorrectly misleads the team and breaks audit trails.
A status that communicates its current state in the lifecycle.

Work is scoped and committed to but not yet started. A "To Do" item has a backlog entry, possibly a story document, but no branch and no code. It is in the queue waiting to be picked up in a session.
No branch exists for this work
No code has been written
The item may or may not have been estimated
Moving from To Do → Implement requires a scope commit on a story branch

The item is actively being worked on. In RaiSE's Jira workflow, "In Progress" is expressed as phase-specific statuses: Design, Plan, Implement. The sub-statuses communicate which phase of the lifecycle is active.
The design document is being written. The code has been read (gemba walk). No implementation has started.
The task decomposition is in progress. Design is complete and approved.

The item cannot proceed due to an external dependency, missing information, or an unresolved decision. Blocked is not a vague catch-all — it requires a documented blocker reason and a resolution path.
A blocker reason is documented (in Jira comment or story journal)
A resolution path is identified (even if "waiting for X")
Moving from Blocked → previous status requires the blocker to be documented as resolved

The implementation is complete (all gates pass) and the work is being reviewed. This includes architecture review, quality review, and human review of the pull/merge request. No new feature code should be written during review — only fixes to review findings.
All automated gates pass (tests, lint, format, types)

All acceptance criteria are met. Tests pass. Retrospective is complete. The story is merged. The Jira issue is in Done. Done means observable value was delivered and the team has extracted learnings. A story that is "technically done" but without a retrospective is not Done in RaiSE — it is incomplete.

The work was decided not to pursue. This is a terminal state with a different meaning than Done — it signals that the value was not delivered, and the reason should be documented. Cancelled items contribute to "waste" metrics and should inform future planning.
Using "In Progress" for months without movement. This masks stale work.
Using Backlog as "won't do". The backlog is a queue, not an archive.
Marking Done without retrospective. This loses learnings and breaks the pattern system.
Reopening Done items. Create a new story or bugfix instead.
Use Blocked if truly stuck.

Status transitions are not free-form. Each transition has preconditions that must be satisfied. These rules exist because a transition communicates a commitment — moving to "Review" means gates pass, moving to "Done" means retrospective exists. Violating the rules creates false signals that mislead the team and corrupt reporting.
Each transition has preconditions that must be satisfied.
A transition communicates a commitment — moving to "Review" means gates pass, moving to "Done" means retrospective exists.
Violating the rules creates false signals that mislead the team and corrupt reporting.
Scope commit exists on the story branch. The scope commit is the evidence of start. Without it, "in progress" is a lie — no artifact exists.
The scope commit contains `scope.md` (in-scope, out-of-scope, done-when) and `story.md` (user story + Gherkin AC).
/rai-story-start creates the branch and scope commit atomically.
Design document approved by human (HITL gate). A design that hasn't been reviewed is a draft, not a decision. The HITL gate ensures a human has read the design and confirmed it matches the intent.
Plan document exists with gate policy. A plan without gate policy is incomplete. Gate policy specifies exact `rai gate check` commands with `--scope` for each task.

All gates pass — tests (scoped), lint, format, types. "All gates pass" means: `rai gate check gate-tests --scope <pkg>`, `gate-lint`, `gate-format`, `gate-types` all exit 0. A commit that breaks any gate is not implementation-complete.
/rai-mr-create runs the full gate suite before creating the MR.
Retrospective document committed (`s{N}.{M}-retrospective.md`). The retrospective is not optional at close. If you skip it, learnings are lost and patterns don't propagate.
MR approved by reviewer.
Branch merged to development branch.
Branch deleted.
/rai-story-close performs the merge, writes retrospective, transitions Jira, deletes branch.

Transitioning from any state to Blocked.
Precondition: Blocker reason documented and resolution path identified.

Moving backward (from Implement back to Design, etc.) is generally not allowed. The correct pattern when implementation reveals a design flaw is: document the finding, update the design doc, continue from where you are (implementation may need partial rollback). Creating a new story to fix the issue found is acceptable.

Moving to Done without merging violates the Review → Done gate. This leads to a stale branch and work that appears complete but is not integrated.

A bugfix is a defect correction workflow with mandatory root cause analysis. Bugs are not just problems to fix — they are process sensors. A bug that reaches production means something in the development process failed to catch it. That failure is as important as the fix itself.
Root cause analysis (5 Whys, Ishikawa, Gemba) is mandatory before planning a fix. A fix without RCA is a patch, not a fix.
PIR (post-incident review) is required after close.

Bugfixes are classified in four ODC-inspired dimensions: trigger (what caused it to appear), impact (what was affected), qualifier (how severe), and activity (which phase missed it). This classification feeds the Post-Incident Review (PIR) and the pattern system.
The bugfix pipeline: start → triage → analyse → plan → fix → review → close → PIR.
